turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, doctor. Well, what brings me in is that... I just keep dodging anything that even smells like my old job. Office buildings, security talks, networking events near the old work sites—I just stay away from all of it. And if people start asking questions about the day it happened, I just... I make some excuse and get out of there. I just can't be around it, and it's starting to get in the way of things.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly describes actively avoiding places, conversations, and reminders related to an event that happened at their old job.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned 'the day it happened'—did something traumatic or frightening occur at your old job that triggered all of this avoidance?
turns.patient_response: Yes, it did. It was... a really bad situation at work. I know I'm here to get help, but I'd honestly rather not get into the exact details of what went down that day just yet, if that's alright. But yes, something very frightening happened, and that's what started all of this.

turns.doctor_question: How long ago did this traumatic event at work happen?
turns.patient_response: Well, it was about a year and seven months ago. This has all been going on since I was fired right after that armed incident.

turns.doctor_question: Besides avoiding reminders of the incident, have you noticed that you've lost interest in or stopped doing things you used to enjoy—like hobbies, socializing with friends, or activities that used to matter to you?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I still do the things I've always enjoyed. I mean, I still see my friends and keep up with my usual hobbies. It's really just... anything connected to that old job that I stay away from. My personal life and the things I do for fun are still pretty much the same.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient confirms avoiding trauma-related reminders by stating that they stay away from anything connected to their old job.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly denies losing interest in activities, stating they still engage in their usual hobbies and see friends as they always have.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about what happened during that armed incident at work?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I do. It happens out of nowhere, really. I’ll just be doing something normal, like washing dishes, or maybe driving past a warehouse gate, and... the scene just pops right back into my head. It comes back so sharp. I can actually hear the panic in people’s voices again, and I feel my chest tighten up, exactly like I’m right back there.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient explicitly confirms experiencing intrusive, sharp traumatic memories and flashbacks that trigger psychological and physiological distress.

turns.doctor_question: Since this incident happened, have you noticed that you're more on edge or jumpy than you used to be—like you startle easily at sudden noises, or find yourself constantly scanning your surroundings for potential threats?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I'd say I am definitely more jumpy now. It's like my body is just waiting for something bad to happen. If a car backfires outside, or a door slams unexpectedly, I jump hard. Even if somebody just touches my shoulder when I don’t see them coming, I startle. And the thing is, my heart just keeps racing long after everyone else has realized it's nothing and moved on. It takes me a long time to calm down from it.

symptom_reasoning.S080: The patient explicitly confirms being jumpy and describes severe auditory and tactile startle reactions with a delayed physiological recovery.

turns.doctor_question: Since the incident, have you noticed that you feel emotionally numb or detached—like you're having a harder time feeling emotions, or things that would normally upset you or make you happy just don't affect you the same way anymore?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I think so. It's... it's hard to explain, but the things that used to really make me happy just don't anymore. I mean, I used to love listening to salsa music, doing a little painting, or cooking a big Sunday dinner for the family. Those things used to really lift me up. But lately... I just go through the motions. I do them, but that good feeling, that joy I used to get from it... it just doesn't come the way it used to.

symptom_reasoning.S076: The patient explicitly confirms an inability to experience positive emotions, noting that activities like music, painting, and cooking no longer bring joy or the good feeling they used to provide.

turns.doctor_question: Have these symptoms—the flashbacks, the jumpiness, the emotional numbness—been happening pretty much continuously since the incident happened, or did they start later on?
turns.patient_response: They've been happening pretty much continuously, yes. It's... well, this has all been going on ever since I was fired right after that armed incident. That was about a year and seven months ago now, and it just hasn't really stopped since then.
